stem: During aseptic wound care involving sites or areas with different contamination levels, which sequencing principle is appropriate?

options.A: Begin at the most contaminated area and move toward cleaner tissue using fresh supplies for each pass.
options.B: Move back and forth between more contaminated and cleaner areas as long as a fresh swab is used each time.
options.C: Clean areas in random order because sterile gloves eliminate the need for a contamination-based sequence.
options.D: Work from the least contaminated area toward the most contaminated area, avoiding transfer back toward cleaner sites.

rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills describes procedure sequencing in aseptic technique as generally following a clean-to-dirty standard, working from the least contaminated toward the most contaminated key parts and sites. This sequence reduces transfer of microorganisms toward cleaner areas. Therefore D is correct. A reverses the sequence, B permits movement back toward cleaner areas, and C incorrectly assumes sterile gloves eliminate the need for planned contamination control.
educational_objective: During aseptic wound care, sequence care from least contaminated to most contaminated areas and avoid carrying contamination back toward cleaner tissue or key sites.
source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / Open RN Nursing Skills
source_document_title: Nursing Skills, 2nd edition — Chapter 4 Aseptic Technique

source_claim_supported: Aseptic procedure sequencing generally proceeds from least contaminated to most contaminated sites; sterile gloves do not remove the need for contamination-control sequencing.

source_original.stem: During aseptic wound care involving areas with different contamination levels, which sequence is appropriate?

options.A: Begin at the most contaminated area and move toward cleaner tissue using fresh supplies for each pass.
options.B: Move repeatedly between dirty and clean areas as long as a new swab is used each time.
options.C: Clean areas in random order because sterile gloves eliminate the need for a clean-to-dirty sequence.
options.D: Begin at the least contaminated area and move toward more contaminated tissue without returning used material to cleaner areas.

source_original.rationale: Aseptic wound-care sequencing follows a clean-to-dirty principle: begin with the least contaminated area and move toward more contaminated areas without carrying organisms back to cleaner tissue. Option D is correct. A and B reverse that principle, and C ignores contamination control.
source_original.source_detail: Aseptic sequencing/wound care: proceed from clean to dirty, moving from least contaminated toward more contaminated areas and avoiding transfer of organisms back toward cleaner tissue; use clean/sterile supplies appropriately. Current NCBI Bookshelf Nursing Skills wound-care content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; CDC sources were checked and do not provide a more specific clean-to-dirty wound-sequencing statement. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: transmission precautions, PPE, device/environmental safety, asepsis, identification and infection-prevention activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the clean-to-dirty construct and key D. Generalized the stem from wound-specific wording to aseptic wound-care sites/areas with different contamination levels and aligned D directly with NCBI's least-to-most contaminated sequencing language.

audit_findings.source_authority: NCBI/Open RN Nursing Skills aseptic-technique text; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: Chapter 4 > Table 4.3 > Sequencing and non-touch technique
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item mirrors the source's least-to-most contaminated sequencing rule and does not claim that sterile gloves alone control transfer between contaminated areas.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because it reverses the clean-to-dirty direction.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because repeatedly returning toward cleaner sites defeats the contamination-control sequence.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because sterile gloves do not eliminate planned sequencing/non-touch principles.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D preserves the least-to-most contaminated progression without returning contamination toward cleaner sites.
audit_findings.cueing: All options concern sequence/order during the same aseptic procedure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic technique and contamination prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NCBI Table 4.3, each alternative, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. D remained uniquely correct.
